content_html:
Key Developments

New details have surfaced in the case of a former Cornell University student who alleges she was drugged and sexually assaulted for several hours within the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. The woman, referred to as Jane Doe, was 20 at the time of the alleged incident. She has since filed a civil lawsuit against seven former members of the fraternity and Cornell University, asserting that they failed to protect her and prevent the assault.

Initially, Cornell conducted an internal investigation, resulting in the expulsion or suspension of several individuals involved. However, no criminal charges were brought against the accused at that time. This has now changed, as the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office confirmed on Monday, September 28, that it is reopening the criminal investigation in response to community pressure. The DA's office stated that the woman's sworn statement from November 2024 differed from her allegations in the civil lawsuit, a claim her attorney disputes, stating investigators did not follow up on her initial allegations.

In response to the ongoing concerns, New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced that Cornell University has agreed to retain outside counsel for an independent investigation. Furthermore, on October 1, Governor Hochul signed an executive order appointing New York Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor. Attorney General James will be tasked with investigating the incident and, if warranted, prosecuting any offenses that arise from the investigation, including presenting evidence to a grand jury.

The civil lawsuit details that the woman, already intoxicated, visited a friend at the Chi Phi fraternity house. She alleges that two fraternity members pressured her into consuming what she believed to be ketamine before she was sexually assaulted. The complaint further states that around 1:42 a.m. on the night of the incident, a message was sent in a Chi Phi Snapchat group chat suggesting a woman upstairs was available for sex. The woman claims more individuals entered the room, and the assaults continued until 5:45 a.m. She reported the incident to the university's police department three weeks later, stating, "Once she was emotionally ready, she went to the University police and bravely shared what had occurred to her. She went to the police because she believed that she was the victim of a crime," according to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra.

Key Takeaways

  • A former Cornell student has filed a civil lawsuit alleging she was drugged and gang-raped by fraternity members in October 2024.
  • The Tompkins County District Attorney's Office has reopened the criminal investigation into the allegations following community pressure.
  • New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to investigate and potentially prosecute the case.

Why It Matters

This case highlights significant concerns regarding campus safety, fraternity conduct, and the handling of sexual assault allegations within university systems. The reopening of the criminal investigation and the appointment of a special prosecutor signal a serious escalation and a renewed effort to ensure accountability. The involvement of the New York Attorney General's office underscores the gravity of the situation and the potential for systemic issues to be addressed, both at the university and within the broader context of addressing sexual violence on college campuses.
